page_title: CHIP-8 in Common Lisp: The CPU

sources.section: Build your own Emulator / Virtual Machine

summary.title: CHIP-8 in Common Lisp: The CPU
summary.one_liner: Learn how to structure a CHIP-8 emulator's CPU state, main loop, instruction dispatch, and a define-instruction macro for decoding opcodes in Common Lisp.
takeaways: Model the CHIP-8 state (registers, index, program counter, stack, memory) as a Lisp struct with type declarations for speed and runtime checks.
Run the emulator in a loop that executes a batch of cycles then sleeps, targeting about 500 cycles per second.
Each cycle reads a 2-byte big-endian instruction, advances the program counter, and dispatches via a case on nibble masks, since CHIP-8 opcodes don't map cleanly to a function table.
Write a define-instruction macro that parses an argument list like (_ r (mask 2)) into ldb bindings so instruction definitions read like the reference docs.
summary.summary: The author walks through a CHIP-8 emulator written in Common Lisp, starting with the main chip struct, registers, stack, memory, and the flag register accessor. It covers reset and ROM loading, a run-cpu loop that batches cycles with sleeps, and emulate-cycle which fetches and dispatches instructions. The post finishes by building a define-instruction macro that generates argument bindings from a descriptive argument list, illustrated with the RND instruction. The article is the first in a series, with graphics, input, sound, and debugging covered in later posts.
